Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A distraught, sobbing Afghan Taliban member begged the court for mercy, but got none as an unmoved federal judge here Monday handed down maximum life sentences for convictions on drug trafficking and narco-terrorism charges. A guard watches over a pile of burning drugs in Kabul, Afghanistan, on June 25, 2008. Khan Mohammed, 38, of Nangarhar Province became the first person convicted and sentenced in the United States under a 2006 law that increased the penalty for a defendant found to be involved  with terrorism and distributing illegal drugs. Mohammed, who had been extradited from Afghanistan, was convicted by a jury in May of plotting a rocket attack on U.S. military forces and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. He also was found guilty of distributing between $1 million and $3 million worth of heroin into the United States "to kill Americans as part of a jihad." Mohammed's court-appointed lawyer, conceding that "what he did was wrong," urged U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to be lenient and sentence his client to only 20 years in prison. Then the full-bearded Mohammed, dressed in an orange jailhouse jumpsuit, addressed the judge. With tears streaming down his face, and choking back his words, he begged for only one or two years. "I have little children and a woman. They depend on me," Mohammed began. "I'm so worried about them." His lengthy emotional appeal went on to include his reason for selling opium. "In my village that's how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium," he said. Justice Department prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz, however, urged the court to "send a message of deterrence," and warned against "the confluence of drug trafficking and terrorism." "No, he's not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he's not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world," Stiglitz told the judge. "But this is where the rubber meets the road." Bin Laden is the head of al Qaeda, while Escobar, who died in 1993, was the most powerful of Colombian drug lords. "Afghanistan is ground zero for opium, and an almost limitless source of funds to the Taliban," he argued. Kollar-Kotelly agreed fully with the prosecutors, and strongly admonished the Taliban defendant. "You were convicted 99 percent by your own words," the judge declared, as she recalled how a "courageous" Afghan police chief wore an undercover wire to record Mohammed's plotting. "The fact that no one died is only because you didn't get the missiles you wanted," she said. "In 2006, you celebrated the Americans' use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause," the judge continued. "Because of your undiluted hatred for the United States, you might well have launched other attacks had you not been arrested." She added, "Terrorists stand unique among criminals. Deterrence is very important here." Then, concluding dramatically, the judge turned directly to the defendant. "I heard your concerns for your family but no acceptance of responsibility for your action," the judge said. "Defendants often express worry for their families, but if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently."

outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — An Afghan Taliban member wept and pleaded for compassion Monday, but a federal judge in Washington remained unswayed and imposed the maximum sentence of life imprisonment for drug-trafficking and narco-terrorism convictions.

In a related image, a guard stands near a heap of drugs being burned in Kabul, Afghanistan, on June 25, 2008.

Khan Mohammed, a 38-year-old resident of Afghanistan’s Nangarhar Province, became the first defendant convicted and sentenced in the United States under a 2006 statute that established tougher punishment for people involved in both terrorism and the distribution of illegal narcotics.

Mohammed was extradited from Afghanistan. In May, a jury found him guilty of planning a rocket strike against U.S. troops and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. Jurors also convicted him of arranging to send heroin valued at between $1 million and $3 million into the United States “to kill Americans as part of a jihad.”

Acknowledging that his client’s conduct was wrong, Mohammed’s court-appointed attorney asked U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to show leniency and impose a prison term of only 20 years.

Mohammed then spoke directly to the court. Wearing an orange prison jumpsuit and a full beard, he struggled to speak as tears ran down his face. He asked to receive a sentence of just one or two years.

“I have little children and a woman. They depend on me,” he said. “I’m so worried about them.”

During his extended and emotional plea, Mohammed also explained why he had sold opium. He said that in his village, dealing in the drug was necessary to earn a living and that every household was involved with opium.

Federal prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz took the opposite position, asking the judge to deliver a deterrent message and emphasizing the danger created when terrorism and narcotics trafficking intersect.

Stiglitz said Mohammed was neither terrorism’s equivalent of Osama bin Laden nor the drug trade’s equivalent of Pablo Escobar, but argued that his case represented the point at which the two threats became a practical reality.

Bin Laden leads al Qaeda. Escobar, who died in 1993, was Colombia’s most powerful drug lord.

The prosecutor described Afghanistan as the center of global opium production and said the drug provides the Taliban with a virtually unlimited stream of money.

Kollar-Kotelly accepted the prosecution’s arguments and sharply rebuked Mohammed. She told him that his conviction rested “99 percent” on his own statements, noting that a “courageous” Afghan police chief had secretly worn a recording device while Mohammed discussed his plans.

The judge said no one was killed only because Mohammed failed to obtain the missiles he sought.

She also recalled that in 2006 he had celebrated Americans’ use of the opium, viewing the resulting harm as part of a jihad. According to Kollar-Kotelly, Mohammed understood the damage the drug could inflict.

The judge further said that Mohammed’s unrestrained hatred of the United States suggested he might have carried out additional attacks if authorities had not arrested him. She stressed that terrorists occupy a distinct category among criminals and that deterrence was especially significant in this case.

At the end of the hearing, Kollar-Kotelly addressed Mohammed directly. She said she had listened to his fears about his family but had heard no acknowledgment of responsibility for what he had done.

Defendants frequently voice concern for their relatives, she added, but they might make different choices if they considered the effects of their conduct before acting.

A jury found Mohammed guilty of plotting a rocket attack against U.S. forces and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. He was also convicted of arranging to distribute as much as $3 million worth of heroin in the United States.

Khan Mohammed, an Afghan Taliban member, was prosecuted in U.S. federal court for conspiring to attack Jalalabad Airfield, a facility used by American and coalition forces in Afghanistan. Prosecutors said Mohammed sought rockets and other weapons for the planned assault and intended to kill U.S. military personnel stationed at the base. The plot was disrupted before it could be carried out.

The case also involved Mohammed’s efforts to traffic large quantities of heroin. According to the government, he understood that the drugs would be transported to the United States and planned to use the proceeds to obtain weapons and support jihadist operations. His conduct therefore connected Afghanistan’s narcotics trade directly with terrorist violence.

Federal prosecutors charged Mohammed under a 2006 statute that made it a crime to distribute drugs, or attempt to do so, while intending or knowing that the proceeds would benefit a terrorist organization or terrorist activity. The law was designed to target “narco-terrorism,” in which drug trafficking serves as a source of financing for insurgent or extremist groups. Mohammed became the first defendant to be convicted under the provision.

At sentencing, Mohammed asked the court for mercy. His attorneys urged the judge to consider his personal circumstances and impose a punishment less severe than life imprisonment. Prosecutors, however, emphasized the gravity of both the planned attack and the heroin conspiracy, arguing that his actions threatened American service members and demonstrated how drug profits could be used to sustain terrorism.

The court imposed the maximum punishment, sentencing Mohammed to life in prison on the principal counts. The sentence reflected the seriousness with which the U.S. justice system viewed the combination of narcotics trafficking and terrorist activity. As the first conviction and sentence under the 2006 law, the case established an important precedent and sent a forceful warning that those who use the international drug trade to finance attacks against the United States may face the harshest penalties available in federal court.

counterfactuals.output:
# Afghan Taliban member sentenced to life in U.S. narco-terrorism case

**WASHINGTON —** An Afghan man linked to the Taliban was sentenced to life in federal prison for trafficking heroin and planning to use the proceeds to support attacks against U.S. and Afghan forces, the Justice Department said.

Khan Mohammed received two concurrent life sentences in U.S. District Court in Washington after being convicted of narco-terrorism and distributing heroin with the intent to import it into the United States.

Federal prosecutors said Mohammed sought to sell large quantities of heroin and use the profits to purchase rockets and other weapons for Taliban attacks. During recorded conversations with undercover informants, he discussed targeting coalition forces and an airfield in Afghanistan, according to evidence presented at trial.

Mohammed was captured in Afghanistan in 2006 and later transferred to the United States to face charges. A federal jury convicted him in 2008.

The case marked the first conviction under a U.S. federal narco-terrorism law that makes it a crime to engage in drug trafficking while knowingly providing financial or material support to a terrorist organization or terrorist activity, the Justice Department said.

Officials described the prosecution as an example of the connection between Afghanistan’s narcotics trade and militant violence.

Mohammed will serve his sentence in the federal prison system. Because there is no parole in the federal system, the life term means he is expected to remain incarcerated for the rest of his life.

counterfactuals.output:
Khan Mohammed, an Afghan drug trafficker, was sentenced in December 2008 to two concurrent life terms by U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly in Washington. He was the first person convicted under the 2006 federal narco-terrorism statute, which punishes drug trafficking intended to finance terrorist activity. A jury found that Mohammed planned to sell heroin for importation into the United States and use the proceeds to support Taliban attacks on U.S. forces in Afghanistan.

Speaking through an interpreter, Mohammed asked for mercy, acknowledging involvement in drugs but denying that he was a terrorist. He appealed to the judge on behalf of his family and maintained that his talk about helping the Taliban did not amount to a genuine terrorist commitment.

The prosecutor countered that Mohammed’s own recorded statements showed he was ready and willing to use heroin profits to buy weapons and support attacks against American soldiers. The government argued that the danger lay not merely in completed attacks but in his demonstrated willingness to combine narcotics trafficking with violence against U.S. personnel.

Kollar-Kotelly said the trial evidence was overwhelming and treated both aspects of the conduct as exceptionally grave: sending heroin into the United States and helping finance attacks on Americans abroad. She rejected the effort to portray Mohammed’s Taliban-related statements as empty boasting, noting that he had repeatedly discussed using drug proceeds to obtain rockets and other weapons. The judge also emphasized deterrence, saying a severe sentence was necessary to warn others who might consider financing terrorism through the drug trade.

counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON —** An Afghan man convicted of plotting a rocket attack on an American military installation and trafficking heroin to support the Taliban broke down in sobs as he pleaded for mercy, asking a federal judge to imprison him for only “one or two years.”

Instead, U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly imposed the maximum punishment: two life sentences.

Khan Mohammed, an Afghan national linked to the Taliban, was sentenced in federal court in Washington after being convicted of narco-terrorism and international heroin trafficking. Prosecutors said Mohammed planned to attack Jalalabad Airfield in eastern Afghanistan, where American and Afghan personnel were stationed, and agreed to sell heroin while understanding that the proceeds would help finance Taliban operations.

The case marked the first conviction under a federal narco-terrorism statute aimed at people who use drug trafficking to benefit terrorist organizations.

Mohammed wept as he addressed the court through an interpreter. He appealed to the judge for a sharply reduced sentence, spoke of his family and asked to be allowed to return to Afghanistan after serving a year or two. His plea stood in stark contrast to the government’s account of him as a willing Taliban operative prepared to combine narcotics trafficking with lethal violence.

Kollar-Kotelly rejected the request. She imposed life imprisonment on each of the two principal counts, the harshest sentence permitted by law. The terms were ordered to run concurrently.

Prosecutors said Mohammed had discussed acquiring and firing rockets at Jalalabad Airfield in an effort to kill U.S. and Afghan troops. In secretly recorded conversations, he also negotiated a heroin transaction and acknowledged that the drug business could support the Taliban’s jihad against American forces.

The government argued that the combination made Mohammed particularly dangerous: He was not merely a drug trafficker or a political sympathizer, prosecutors said, but someone prepared to use the heroin trade as a source of money for an armed insurgency.

Defense lawyers portrayed him differently. They described Mohammed as an impoverished, poorly educated Afghan villager who had been drawn into sweeping conversations and schemes encouraged by government informants. They argued that his rhetoric exceeded his actual ability and that he lacked the means to carry out the attack.

Jurors rejected that defense, finding that Mohammed intended to distribute heroin while knowing or intending that the proceeds would provide value to the Taliban. They also accepted evidence that his drug dealings were connected to plans for violence against U.S. personnel.

Mohammed was captured in Afghanistan in 2006 and transferred to the United States for prosecution. His trial and conviction gave federal authorities an early test of the narco-terrorism law, which allows prosecutors to seek severe penalties when drug trafficking is tied to terrorism.

At sentencing, the judge said the evidence established far more than idle talk. Mohammed’s willingness to help arrange a rocket strike and to sell heroin for the Taliban, she concluded, justified the maximum term.

The hearing ended with Mohammed still visibly distraught. His request for a brief sentence denied, he was led from the courtroom to begin serving life in federal prison.

counterfactuals.output:
## Federal Judge Denies Leniency to Afghan Drug Trafficker, Citing Opium’s Role in Taliban Terrorism

**WASHINGTON —** A federal judge in Washington rejected Khan Mohammed’s request for leniency, stressing that his heroin-trafficking activities were inseparable from efforts to finance the Taliban and support terrorist attacks against U.S. and coalition forces in Afghanistan.

Mohammed, an Afghan national, was convicted under the federal narco-terrorism statute after prosecutors presented evidence that he planned to distribute large quantities of heroin while directing proceeds to the Taliban. The case was among the first to use the law, which targets drug trafficking carried out to provide financial or material support to terrorist organizations.

In declining to reduce Mohammed’s punishment, the judge emphasized the seriousness of using Afghanistan’s opium trade as a source of terrorist financing. The court found that his conduct went beyond conventional drug trafficking: heroin sales were intended not only to generate personal profit but also to strengthen an insurgent movement engaged in violence against Americans and their allies.

Evidence at trial showed that Mohammed discussed sending heroin to the United States and using drug revenue to assist the Taliban. Prosecutors also linked him to plans for attacks on an airfield used by U.S. and coalition personnel in Afghanistan.

The ruling highlighted the broader relationship between Afghanistan’s narcotics economy and the country’s long-running insurgency. For years, the Taliban benefited from opium cultivation and heroin production through taxation, protection payments and direct involvement in trafficking networks. That revenue helped purchase weapons, pay fighters and sustain operations in areas where the central government exercised limited control.

The judge concluded that this connection magnified the harm caused by Mohammed’s crimes. Heroin trafficking already carried devastating consequences for users and communities, the court reasoned, but channeling the proceeds toward terrorist violence made the offense particularly grave.

Mohammed had sought a more lenient outcome based on mitigating circumstances. The court, however, determined that those considerations did not outweigh the nature of his conduct, the need to protect the public and the importance of deterring others from using narcotics profits to finance terrorism.

The decision reinforces the federal government’s view that drug trafficking and terrorism can form part of the same criminal enterprise. In Afghanistan, where opium historically generated billions of dollars within the illicit economy, narcotics revenue provided armed groups with a durable funding stream that was difficult to disrupt through traditional counterterrorism measures alone.

By refusing leniency, the court treated Mohammed’s case as more than a prosecution of an individual trafficker. It cast the offense as part of a wider system in which opium becomes heroin, heroin becomes money, and that money helps sustain terrorist organizations and attacks.
